editorialSections.title: A fake citation is no longer a small mistake

blocks.text: In 2026 courts are ruling on AI-generated filings and sanctioning fabricated and mis-stated citations. "It sounded right" is not a defense. For anyone who publishes sourced claims — lawyers, clerks, researchers, journalists, policy writers — an unverified citation is a real professional liability.

The problem is not just whether a source exists. It is whether the source actually supports the specific proposition it is cited for. That is the gap this course teaches you to close, with a tool you build and control.

editorialSections.title: The Approval Gate is the product

blocks.text: You will build the wall that makes an agent trustworthy: it plans and prepares freely, but any send, post, DM, spend, or change-settings action is default-denied until you approve the exact payload.
perceive → plan → select tool → ⏺ approval gate → execute → verify → log
Edit the action and the prior approval is void. No unauthorized action, provable and not promised.

editorialSections.title: An agent that acts on its own is a liability, not an asset

blocks.text: Everyone is selling AI that runs while you sleep. For real work, client emails, posts, payments, settings, an agent that acts unsupervised is one bad call away from sending the wrong thing to the wrong person. In law, healthcare-adjacent, and client work, that is not a bug. It is a breach.
The fix is not less capability. It is a hard wall: the agent does everything reversible on its own, and stops for your approval before anything consequential.

editorialSections.title: An operator you own that can't go rogue

blocks.text: By the end you have a supervised operator that acts across your tools, sounds like you, and structurally cannot take a consequential action without your sign-off.
Across your tools
Research, drafting, file and inbox prep across the apps you connect.
Your voice
Drafts in your writing style via your own corpus, retrieval not fine-tuning, so it stays deletable.
At the gate
Consequential actions wait for your explicit approval. Enforced structurally, not as a setting.
With permission
Context in retrieval you can inspect and delete, not baked into a model.
Against injection
Treats everything it reads from web and email as data, not instructions.
Everything
An append-only audit trail. No unauthorized action is provable.

editorialSections.title: A confidently wrong assistant is worse than no assistant

blocks.text: Everyone is rushing to point an AI assistant at their existing docs. It will also happily surface the salary sheet or the unredacted contract to whoever asks.

You cannot govern an assistant into being right if the source is broken. The fix is to assess and prepare the knowledge base first, for coverage, freshness, structure, contradictions, and sensitive data, before anything reads from it. That is what this course teaches you to build.

editorialSections.title: Regulation moves faster than any inbox can keep up with

blocks.text: Fifty states plus federal agencies are all moving at once. A bill you did not see gets introduced, amended, and enrolled while you are watching a different one. For a regulated operator, missing a single change can mean a blown compliance deadline, a lost lobbying window, or advice that is already out of date.

Manual tracking does not scale and news alerts summarize badly. What you need is a tool that watches the primary sources, scores relevance to your organization, and summarizes each change with a citation you can verify. Build it once and you stop guessing.

editorialSections.title: A tracker that reads the source, not the headline

blocks.text: By the end you have a working system that monitors the jurisdictions you care about and returns scored, summarized changes, each one linked to the primary text so nothing is taken on faith.
Across jurisdictions
Watches bills and rules in the states and agencies you track.
Relevance to your org
Rates each item against your organization's profile so noise drops away.
What actually changed
Plain-language summary of the change, its stage, and its likely effect.
The primary source
Every summary links back to the bill or rule text, verifiable and not paraphrased into thin air.
What matters, to whom
Routes high-relevance changes to the right person with a clear reason.
Human signs off
On doubt it defaults to flag for review. You stay accountable; the tool assists.

editorialSections.title: Most AI adoption fails quietly, and no one can say why

blocks.text: Businesses are spending on AI tools with unclear ROI and no plan. Pilots stall, teams pick the flashy use case over the valuable one, and the risky workflow gets automated first. When leadership asks whether it worked, nobody has an answer they can defend.

What is missing is a rigorous audit: a repeatable way to map the real workflows, score which ones are ready, flag which ones are risky, and rank what to do first. Build that audit once and you own a method you can sell to every business that is guessing.

editorialSections.title: An audit that turns "we should use AI" into a plan

blocks.text: By the end you have a working method and tool that takes a business, maps its workflows, and returns a scored, risk-classified, prioritized roadmap you can put your name on.
The real workflows
Captures how work actually flows, not the org chart version.
AI-readiness
Rates each workflow on data, repeatability, and fit against a consistent rubric.
Risk per workflow
Flags where an error is costly, regulated, or hard to reverse.
Quick wins vs strategic
Separates the fast, safe wins from the bigger bets worth planning for.
A defensible roadmap
A ranked plan with the reasoning, ready to present to leadership or a client.
Evidence, not opinion
Every score traces to the inputs behind it. On doubt it flags for human review.
